before.title: Software and data

after.classroomConnection: Information helps only when people can find it, trust it and use it for the intended decision.

before.title: Conservation research and population ecology
before.summary: Find out whether an intervention helps a wild population recover.
before.explanation: Conservation researchers connect observations of individual animals to changes in a population. They plan what to measure, compare outcomes and explain what the evidence can and cannot establish.

tasks.title: Plan a comparison
tasks.detail: Choose measures of survival, breeding and population change, and decide what to compare them with.

tasks.title: Follow animals after release
tasks.detail: Record observations over time, accounting for animals that are difficult to detect.

tasks.title: Interpret the evidence
tasks.detail: Ask whether results reflect the intervention, environmental conditions or other explanations.

before.classroomConnection: Survival and reproduction at different life stages affect population change. A successful release alone does not establish population recovery.

after.title: Conservation research and population ecology
after.summary: Investigate changes in living populations and habitats using repeatable observations.
after.explanation: Conservation researchers choose ecological questions, plan comparisons and interpret evidence about living populations and their habitats. Measures can include survival, reproduction, abundance or vegetation; the choice depends on the question.

tasks.title: Plan a comparison
tasks.detail: Choose relevant ecological measures and a defensible comparison.

tasks.title: Observe consistently
tasks.detail: Record organisms and environmental conditions using repeatable methods.

tasks.title: Interpret the evidence
tasks.detail: Consider detection limits and alternative explanations before drawing conclusions.

after.classroomConnection: A visible change does not by itself establish the cause of ecological recovery.

before.title: Process engineering
before.summary: Design and test the steps that separate useful materials from a mixture.
before.explanation: Process engineers connect chemistry to equipment and operating conditions. They use calculations, models and test results to decide how a process should work, then help troubleshoot what happens when it is scaled up.

tasks.title: Compare separation steps
tasks.detail: Evaluate how different treatment stages affect recovery, purity and resource use.

tasks.title: Check the balances
tasks.detail: Account for material entering and leaving each stage, using models and measurements.

tasks.title: Test and improve
tasks.detail: Use pilot or demonstration results to improve designs and support commissioning.

before.classroomConnection: Concentration, mixtures and quantitative chemical change become practical questions about recovery, purity, water use and scale.

after.title: Process engineering
after.summary: Use chemistry, measurements and engineering constraints to design and improve industrial processes.
after.explanation: Process engineers compare operating conditions and test results, model how materials move and change, and work with other specialists to improve a process. The relevant process may involve separation, treatment or fluid handling.

tasks.title: Define the process
tasks.detail: Identify materials, desired outcomes and operating constraints.

tasks.title: Compare evidence
tasks.detail: Use measurements and calculations to compare possible conditions or stages.

tasks.title: Test and improve
tasks.detail: Evaluate results and identify changes that need further testing.

after.classroomConnection: Material properties and quantitative comparisons help explain how a process behaves and where a model is incomplete.
